title: ABC Adventures
description: A child-friendly literacy guide that helps young learners recognize letters, sounds, and simple words through play.
contentHtml:
ABC Adventures

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This activity helps young children begin their reading journey through letters, sounds, pictures, movement, and simple conversation.

What children will learn

  • Recognize common letters.
  • Connect letters with sounds.
  • Say simple words clearly.
  • Build confidence while learning.

Warm-up activity

Ask the child to sing the alphabet slowly. After singing, choose five letters and ask the child to find objects around them that begin with those letters.

Letter sound game

Pick one letter, say the sound, and ask the child to repeat it. Example: “B says /b/ as in ball, baby, bag.” Let the child clap once each time they hear the sound.

Picture-word match

Draw or show pictures such as apple, ball, cup, dog, egg, fish, and goat. Ask the child to say the word and identify the first letter.

Mini practice

  1. Trace five letters with a finger.
  2. Say the letter name.
  3. Say the letter sound.
  4. Say one word that begins with the letter.

Reflection questions

  • What letter did you enjoy today?
  • What word was easy for you?
  • What word do you want to try again?

For parents and teachers

Use encouragement, repetition, and play. Do not shame a child for forgetting letters. Young children learn best when reading feels safe, warm, and fun.

title: Numbers Fun
description: A playful numeracy guide that helps children count, compare, group, and understand numbers in daily life.
contentHtml:
Numbers Fun

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children enjoy numbers through counting, movement, toys, food items, and simple household objects.

What children will learn

  • Count objects from 1 to 20.
  • Understand more, less, and equal.
  • Match numbers to real items.
  • Build patience and confidence.

Counting around me

Ask the child to count spoons, shoes, cups, pencils, or toys. Let them touch each object as they count so they understand that every number represents one item.

More or less game

Place three objects on one side and five objects on another side. Ask: “Which side has more?” Then change the objects and repeat.

Movement counting

  • Jump 5 times.
  • Clap 10 times.
  • Touch your head 3 times.
  • Take 7 tiny steps.

Mini activity

Give the child numbers 1–10 on small cards. Ask them to arrange the cards in order, then place the correct number of objects under each card.

Reflection questions

  • What number did you count up to today?
  • Which number was hard?
  • Where do you see numbers at home or school?

For parents and teachers

Avoid rushing. Celebrate small progress. Children need repetition before numbers become meaningful.

title: Colors and Shapes
description: A creative early-learning resource for identifying colors, shapes, patterns, and objects in the child’s environment.
contentHtml:
Colors and Shapes

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This activity helps young children notice colors and shapes in everyday life while developing language, attention, and observation skills.

What children will learn

  • Name common colors.
  • Recognize circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles.
  • Describe objects clearly.
  • Use creativity through drawing and sorting.

Color hunt

Choose one color and ask the child to find three things with that color. Example: “Find three blue things.” Let the child point, name, and describe each item.

Shape hunt

Look around the room. Ask: “What looks like a circle? What looks like a rectangle?” Use plates, doors, books, windows, clocks, and boxes.

Draw and color

  1. Draw one circle, one square, and one triangle.
  2. Color each shape differently.
  3. Ask the child to describe the picture.
  4. Let the child make a simple house, car, or flower using shapes.

Pattern practice

Create a pattern: red-blue-red-blue. Ask the child what comes next. Try shape patterns too: circle-square-circle-square.

Reflection questions

  • What is your favorite color?
  • What shape was easy to find?
  • What can you build with shapes?

For parents and teachers

Use daily objects instead of expensive learning tools. Children learn faster when the lesson connects to things they already see.

title: Good Manners
description: A practical character-building guide that teaches respect, kindness, polite words, and responsible behavior.
contentHtml:
Good Manners

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Good manners help children build respect, friendship, confidence, and peaceful relationships at home, school, and in the community.

What are good manners?

Good manners are kind and respectful ways of speaking and behaving. They show people that we value them and care about their feelings.

Important polite words

  • Please
  • Thank you
  • Excuse me
  • I am sorry
  • May I?
  • You are welcome

Everyday examples

  • Greet people respectfully.
  • Wait for your turn.
  • Do not interrupt when someone is speaking.
  • Say thank you when someone helps you.
  • Apologize when you hurt someone.

Role-play activity

Practice three scenes: asking for help, apologizing to a friend, and thanking a teacher. Let children act out both the wrong way and the better way.

Reflection questions

  • Which polite word do you use often?
  • Which polite word do you need to practice?
  • How do you feel when someone speaks kindly to you?

For parents and teachers

Children copy adults. Model the same manners you want them to use. Correct with calmness, not embarrassment.

title: My Feelings
description: A mental wellbeing guide that helps children name, understand, and express feelings safely.
contentHtml:
My Feelings

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide helps children understand that feelings are normal and can be expressed safely.

What are feelings?

Feelings are emotions we experience inside. We may feel happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, lonely, proud, or worried. Feelings are not bad, but our actions must be safe.

Common feelings

  • Happy: when something good happens.
  • Sad: when we lose, miss, or feel hurt.
  • Angry: when something feels unfair.
  • Scared: when we feel unsafe or unsure.
  • Worried: when we keep thinking about a problem.

Healthy ways to express feelings

  • Use words: “I feel sad because…”
  • Draw the feeling.
  • Talk to a trusted adult.
  • Take deep breaths.
  • Ask for a break.

Feeling thermometer

Ask the child to rate their feeling from 1 to 5. 1 means calm. 5 means very strong. Then ask what would help them move down one step.

Reflection questions

  • What feeling did you have today?
  • Where did you feel it in your body?
  • Who can you talk to when feelings are too big?

For parents and teachers

Do not dismiss feelings with “stop crying” or “you are fine.” Help the child name the emotion, feel safe, and choose a better action.

title: Safety First
description: A child protection and personal safety guide that teaches safe boundaries, trusted adults, and emergency help-seeking.
contentHtml:
Safety First

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. This guide teaches children how to stay safe, speak up, and ask for help when something feels wrong.

What safety means

Safety means protecting your body, mind, feelings, and environment. Every child deserves to feel safe at home, school, online, and in the community.

Body safety rules

  • Your body belongs to you.
  • No one should touch private parts except for health or hygiene reasons with proper adult support.
  • You can say “No” to unsafe touch.
  • Unsafe secrets should be reported.
  • Tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong.

Trusted adults

A trusted adult is someone who listens, protects, and helps you without making you feel afraid. Examples may include a parent, teacher, school counsellor, caregiver, nurse, or responsible family member.

Safety circle activity

Ask the child to draw a circle and write the names of three trusted adults they can talk to if they feel unsafe.

Emergency practice

  • Know your full name.
  • Know your parent or caregiver’s phone number if possible.
  • Know where to go for help in school.
  • Never follow a stranger without permission.

For parents and teachers

Teach safety calmly, without frightening the child. Children must know they will not be blamed for reporting unsafe behavior.

title: Healthy Habits
description: A practical wellbeing guide that teaches sleep, food, hygiene, movement, screen balance, and daily self-care.
contentHtml:
Healthy Habits

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Healthy habits help children grow, learn, play, and manage emotions better.

Why habits matter

Small daily habits affect energy, mood, focus, confidence, and health. Children do not need perfect routines. They need simple, repeated actions that support their wellbeing.

Important habits

  • Sleep early and wake up refreshed.
  • Eat balanced meals when possible.
  • Drink water.
  • Brush teeth and bathe regularly.
  • Move the body through play or exercise.
  • Take breaks from screens.

My healthy day checklist

  1. I washed my hands.
  2. I drank water.
  3. I moved my body.
  4. I ate something nourishing.
  5. I rested when I was tired.
  6. I spoke kindly to myself.

Activity

Ask the child to choose one habit to practice for seven days. Keep a small chart and tick each day they try.

Reflection questions

  • What healthy habit is easy for me?
  • What habit do I need help with?
  • How does my body feel after rest and good food?

For parents and teachers

Make routines visible and simple. Avoid using food, sleep, or body size as shame-based discipline.

title: Story Time
description: A reading and reflection guide that helps children learn values, emotions, and problem-solving through stories.
contentHtml:
Story Time

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Stories help children build language, imagination, empathy, and decision-making.

Why stories are powerful

Children learn from characters. A story can teach kindness, courage, patience, honesty, safety, and emotional awareness without sounding like a lecture.

How to read a story

  • Look at the title and picture first.
  • Ask what the child thinks the story is about.
  • Read slowly.
  • Pause to ask questions.
  • Let the child retell the story in their own words.

Story reflection questions

  • Who is the main character?
  • What problem did the character face?
  • How did the character feel?
  • What choice did the character make?
  • What would you have done?

Create your own story

Ask the child to create a short story about a child who helps a friend. The story should have a beginning, a problem, a helpful action, and an ending.

Mini activity

Draw one scene from the story and write or say one lesson learned.

For parents and teachers

Do not focus only on reading accuracy. Use stories to build confidence, listening, vocabulary, empathy, and moral reasoning.

title: Reading Club
description: A guide for creating a simple reading habit, discussing books, and building vocabulary with peers.
contentHtml:
Reading Club

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. A reading club helps learners enjoy books, improve vocabulary, and build confidence in speaking.

What is a reading club?

A reading club is a small group of learners who read, discuss, ask questions, and share lessons from books, articles, stories, or poems.

Club rules

  • Respect every reader.
  • Do not laugh at mistakes.
  • Take turns speaking.
  • Ask questions kindly.
  • Share one lesson from each reading.

Weekly reading plan

  1. Choose a short text.
  2. Read silently for 10 minutes.
  3. Read one paragraph aloud.
  4. Discuss difficult words.
  5. Share the main lesson.

Vocabulary builder

Each learner writes three new words, their meanings, and one sentence using each word.

Reflection questions

  • What did I learn from today’s reading?
  • What new word can I use this week?
  • How did the story connect to real life?

For teachers

Keep the group safe and encouraging. The goal is not to embarrass weak readers; the goal is to build steady confidence.

title: Mathematics Fun
description: A friendly math confidence guide that helps children practice numbers, addition, subtraction, and problem-solving.
contentHtml:
Mathematics Fun

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Mathematics becomes easier when children practice with real objects, games, and calm guidance.

Why math matters

Math helps us count money, share food, tell time, measure things, compare prices, and solve everyday problems.

Simple addition

Use stones, pencils, beans, or bottle tops. Put 4 items on the table. Add 3 more. Count all together. Explain that 4 + 3 = 7.

Simple subtraction

Place 8 objects on the table. Remove 2. Count what is left. Explain that 8 - 2 = 6.

Math in daily life

  • Count steps while walking.
  • Share snacks equally.
  • Compare which cup has more water.
  • Count coins or notes with guidance.
  • Read numbers on signs and doors.

Activity

Create five real-life math questions. Example: “If I have 5 mangoes and give 2 away, how many remain?”

Reflection questions

  • What math topic feels easy?
  • What topic do I need help with?
  • How can I practice without fear?

For parents and teachers

Do not call a child “bad at math.” Anxiety makes learning harder. Use patience, objects, repetition, and praise for effort.

title: Science Explorers
description: A curiosity-building science resource that encourages observation, questioning, experiments, and safe exploration.
contentHtml:
Science Explorers

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Science helps children ask questions, observe carefully, test ideas, and understand the world.

What is science?

Science is the process of learning about nature, people, animals, plants, weather, materials, health, and technology through observation and evidence.

Explorer mindset

  • Ask: What do I notice?
  • Ask: Why might this happen?
  • Test safely.
  • Record what you see.
  • Explain your findings.

Simple experiment: floating and sinking

Collect safe objects like a spoon, leaf, plastic bottle cap, coin, and small stick. Predict which will float. Place them in water one by one and record what happens.

Observation journal

Choose a plant, cloud, insect, shadow, or water container. Observe it for three days and write or draw what changes.

Reflection questions

  • What surprised me today?
  • What question do I still have?
  • How can science help my community?

Safety note

Children should not mix unknown chemicals, taste experiment materials, use fire, or handle sharp objects without adult supervision.

title: Creative Drawing
description: A gentle creative expression guide that helps children use drawing to communicate ideas, feelings, and stories.
contentHtml:
Creative Drawing

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Drawing helps children express thoughts, feelings, imagination, and stories even before they can write fluently.

Why drawing matters

Drawing builds fine motor skills, focus, creativity, confidence, and emotional expression. A child’s drawing does not need to be perfect to be meaningful.

Today’s drawing ideas

  • Draw your family.
  • Draw your favorite food.
  • Draw a happy place.
  • Draw how you feel today.
  • Draw an animal you like.

Feeling drawing

Ask the child: “If your feeling had a color, what color would it be?” Let them draw the feeling using shapes and colors.

Tell me about it

After drawing, ask the child to explain the picture. Avoid judging the artwork. Ask open questions like, “What is happening here?”

Mini activity

Fold a paper into four boxes. In each box, draw: something I like, someone I love, something I can do, and something I want to learn.

For parents and teachers

Do not over-correct drawings. Creative expression should feel safe. Praise effort, ideas, and storytelling.

title: Public Speaking for Kids
description: A confidence-building guide that teaches children how to speak clearly, organize ideas, and present without fear.
contentHtml:
Public Speaking for Kids

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Public speaking helps children share ideas, build confidence, and communicate respectfully.

Why public speaking matters

Children who practice speaking learn to organize thoughts, make eye contact, use clear words, and express themselves with courage.

Simple speech structure

  1. Greeting: “Good morning everyone.”
  2. Topic: “Today I will speak about…”
  3. Three points: share three clear ideas.
  4. Conclusion: “Thank you for listening.”

Practice tips

  • Stand straight.
  • Speak slowly.
  • Breathe before starting.
  • Look at friendly faces.
  • Practice with a small group first.

One-minute speech activity

Choose one topic: my favorite subject, my role model, why kindness matters, or how to stay safe. Prepare three points and speak for one minute.

Reflection questions

  • What makes speaking in public scary?
  • What helps me feel brave?
  • What topic can I speak about confidently?

For teachers

Do not force ridicule-based presentations. Start with pairs, then small groups, then larger groups. Confidence grows gradually.

title: Leadership for Kids
description: A child-friendly leadership guide focused on responsibility, service, teamwork, decision-making, and integrity.
contentHtml:
Leadership for Kids

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Leadership is not about shouting or controlling people. It is about serving, guiding, taking responsibility, and doing what is right.

Who is a good leader?

A good leader listens, respects others, tells the truth, helps solve problems, and makes choices that protect the group.

Leadership qualities

  • Responsibility
  • Honesty
  • Kindness
  • Courage
  • Teamwork
  • Problem-solving

Leadership at school

  • Help a classmate understand a task.
  • Report bullying or unsafe behavior.
  • Keep promises.
  • Encourage others.
  • Use respectful words even when correcting someone.

Activity: leadership challenge

Choose one helpful action to do this week. Examples: organize books, welcome a new student, help clean the classroom, or support someone who feels left out.

Reflection questions

  • How can I lead without being proud?
  • What problem can I help solve?
  • Who is a leader I admire and why?

For parents and teachers

Give children small responsibilities. Leadership grows when children are trusted, guided, and held accountable.

title: Emotional Intelligence
description: A deeper emotional wellbeing guide that helps young learners understand feelings, empathy, choices, and self-control.
contentHtml:
Emotional Intelligence

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Emotional intelligence means understanding your feelings, managing your actions, and respecting other people’s feelings too.

The four skills

  • Notice: What am I feeling?
  • Name: What is this feeling called?
  • Understand: Why might I feel this way?
  • Choose: What safe action should I take?

Feelings and actions are different

You may feel angry, but you can choose not to insult, hit, or destroy things. You may feel afraid, but you can ask for help and take one brave step.

Empathy practice

Empathy means trying to understand how another person feels. Ask: “How would I feel if this happened to me?”

Self-control tools

  • Pause before reacting.
  • Take three slow breaths.
  • Use words instead of shouting.
  • Walk away from danger.
  • Ask an adult for help.

Reflection questions

  • What feeling is hardest for me to manage?
  • What helps me calm down?
  • How can I show empathy this week?

For parents and teachers

Teach emotional intelligence through real situations. Help children repair harm after mistakes instead of only punishing them.

title: Environmental Awareness
description: A values-based guide that teaches children cleanliness, care for nature, waste reduction, and community responsibility.
contentHtml:
Environmental Awareness

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Caring for the environment means protecting the places where people, animals, and plants live.

What is the environment?

The environment includes air, water, land, plants, animals, homes, schools, roads, and communities around us.

How children can help

  • Do not throw litter on the ground.
  • Use bins when available.
  • Save water.
  • Care for plants.
  • Keep classrooms and playgrounds clean.
  • Reuse items safely when possible.

Clean space activity

Choose one small area, such as a desk, classroom corner, or bedroom space. Clean it, arrange it, and discuss how it feels afterward.

Nature observation

Look at one plant or tree. Notice the leaves, color, shape, and size. Discuss why plants need water, sunlight, soil, and care.

Reflection questions

  • Why should we keep our school clean?
  • What happens when people throw trash everywhere?
  • What one environmental habit can I practice?

For teachers

Use environmental care as a leadership and responsibility lesson. Assign rotating cleanliness roles without using shame or punishment.

title: Kind Words
description: A kindness and communication guide that helps children understand how words affect feelings and relationships.
contentHtml:
Kind Words

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Words can help or hurt. Kind words make people feel seen, respected, encouraged, and safe.

What are kind words?

Kind words are words that show respect, care, patience, and encouragement. They do not insult, mock, threaten, or embarrass others.

Examples of kind words

  • You can try again.
  • I am sorry.
  • Thank you for helping me.
  • Would you like to join us?
  • I like your effort.
  • Are you okay?

Words that hurt

Calling people names, laughing at mistakes, spreading rumors, and shouting insults can make others feel sad, ashamed, or afraid.

Kindness challenge

Say one kind sentence to three people today: a friend, a teacher, and someone at home.

Reflection questions

  • What kind word made me feel good before?
  • Have I ever used words that hurt someone?
  • How can I repair hurtful words?

For parents and teachers

Correct unkind speech early. Teach children to apologize clearly: “I am sorry I said ____. It was not kind. I will try to speak better.”

title: Sharing and Teamwork
description: A social development guide that teaches turn-taking, sharing, helping, and working together.
contentHtml:
Sharing and Teamwork

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Sharing and teamwork help children learn patience, friendship, cooperation, and respect.

What is sharing?

Sharing means allowing others to use, enjoy, or take turns with something. It does not always mean giving everything away. It means learning fairness and kindness.

What is teamwork?

Teamwork means people working together to complete a task, solve a problem, or help one another.

Practice phrases

  • Can I have a turn?
  • You can use it after me.
  • Let us do it together.
  • Thank you for sharing.
  • Please may I join?

Team activity

Give children blocks, paper, or toys and ask them to build something together. One child chooses, one arranges, one counts, and one explains.

Reflection questions

  • How do I feel when someone shares with me?
  • How can I ask for a turn kindly?
  • What can our team do better next time?

For parents and teachers

Young children are still learning impulse control. Teach turn-taking with timers, clear rules, and calm repetition.

title: My Safety Circle
description: A practical protection guide that helps children identify trusted adults and know when to ask for help.
contentHtml:
My Safety Circle

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. Every child needs a safety circle: trusted people they can talk to when they feel worried, confused, unsafe, or hurt.

What is a safety circle?

A safety circle is a small group of trusted adults who listen, protect, guide, and help a child make safe decisions.

Who can be in my safety circle?

  • Parent or caregiver
  • Teacher
  • School counsellor
  • Responsible relative
  • Faith leader or community helper
  • Health worker

When should I talk to my safety circle?

  • When someone touches me in an unsafe way.
  • When someone asks me to keep a bad secret.
  • When I feel scared, threatened, or followed.
  • When I am bullied.
  • When I feel very sad or overwhelmed.

Activity

Draw your hand. On each finger, write one trusted adult. Practice saying: “I need help. Something happened and I want to talk.”

Reflection questions

  • Who listens to me well?
  • Who helps me feel safe?
  • What should I do if the first adult does not listen?

For parents and teachers

Tell children they can keep reporting until someone helps. A child should never be punished for speaking up about safety.

title: Calm Down Toolbox
description: A practical emotional regulation guide that teaches safe calming tools for worry, anger, fear, and overwhelm.
contentHtml:
Calm Down Toolbox

Published by SpeakOut Mental Health Outreach. A calm down toolbox is a set of safe actions a learner can use when feelings become too strong.

When to use this toolbox

Use it when you feel angry, anxious, embarrassed, afraid, overwhelmed, or close to reacting in a way that could hurt yourself or someone else.

Tool 1: Pause and breathe

Breathe in slowly for four counts. Hold for two counts. Breathe out slowly for four counts. Repeat five times.

Tool 2: Name the feeling

Say quietly: “I feel ____ because ____.” Naming the feeling helps the brain slow down.

Tool 3: Grounding

  • Name 5 things you can see.
  • Name 4 things you can touch.
  • Name 3 things you can hear.
  • Name 2 things you can smell.
  • Name 1 safe thing you can do next.

Tool 4: Safe support

Talk to a trusted adult, school counsellor, parent, teacher, or responsible older person when the feeling is too big to handle alone.

Reflection questions

  • What feeling do I need help calming?
  • Which tool works best for me?
  • Who can I talk to when I am overwhelmed?

Important safety note

If a young person feels like harming themselves or someone else, they should tell a trusted adult immediately and get urgent support.
